summaries.example: Imagine a song that makes people want to listen, smile, and protect it from being damaged. A fitting-attitude theory asks whether the song is good because it deserves these positive responses. It also asks whether every reason to like it really shows that it is good. For example, if someone threatens to punish you unless you praise a bad song, that threat may give you a reason to praise it, but it may not make the song good.
summaries.summary: Fitting-attitude theories try to explain value by looking at responses that things deserve. Something may be admirable because it deserves admiration, lovable because it deserves love, or delightful because it deserves enjoyment. Some versions explain general goodness through what is fitting to value. These theories are attractive because they connect many kinds of value and may make value easier to understand. However, philosophers still debate which responses count, who should have them, and whether the explanation goes in the right direction. They also discuss difficult cases: a threat may give someone a reason to praise something bad; valuable things might exist where no one can value them; personal friendships may support partial choices; and explaining “positive” responses may seem to assume value already.
key_ideas: Fitting-attitude theories explain value by asking which human responses are deserved.
Different values may call for different responses: admiration, love, enjoyment, blame, or protection.
Theories disagree about whether the important response is fitting, required, rational, or supported by reasons.
Some philosophers think these theories connect many kinds of value in one pattern.
Critics ask whether the theory handles threats, imaginary worlds without people, favoritism, and circular explanations.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory helps us think carefully about words such as good, admirable, lovable, and valuable. It asks whether value is completely independent of people, merely a description of what people happen to like, or connected to responses that are truly deserved. This can improve discussions about art, friendship, choices, and reasons without assuming that every strong feeling is a good guide.

important_terms.definition: A response, such as admiring, loving, enjoying, or valuing something, that is appropriate or deserved.
A feature of something that makes a certain response to it appropriate or deserved.
The idea that something is good or valuable because it is worthy of a certain response.
The idea that some value facts are basic and cannot be explained using other facts.

questions_to_think_about: Is something good because it deserves praise, or does it deserve praise because it is good?
Can a threat give you a reason to praise something without making it praiseworthy?
Should it ever be appropriate to favor a friend when two choices seem equally good?

summaries.example: Suppose two people can be rescued, and all their features are equal except that one is your close friend. It may be fitting for you to prefer rescuing your friend, even if neither rescue outcome is better overall. This creates the problem of partiality for a theory that explains betterness by what anyone ought to prefer. A different challenge involves a threat: if a demon will harm you unless you admire a worthless object, the threat may be a reason to admire it without making the object admirable. The theory must distinguish reasons that make an attitude appropriate from reasons that merely pressure someone into having it.
summaries.summary: Fitting-attitude (FA) theories explain evaluative facts through normative facts about responses such as admiring, loving, enjoying, blaming, desiring, or valuing. For example, an FA theorist may claim that a person is admirable because admiration toward that person is fitting, or that something is valuable because there are reasons to value it. Contemporary versions usually aim to explain properties and facts themselves, sometimes through grounding: the evaluative fact holds in virtue of the normative fact about a response. This distinguishes FA theory from primitivism, which treats value as basic, and from subjectivism, which explains value through non-normative facts about actual or idealized responses. The entry emphasizes several choices. The theory may concern specific or general value; it may use fittingness or another normative relation; it must determine whose response matters; and it may or may not accept Scanlon-style buck-passing, according to which value passes normative importance to lower-level features that provide reasons. FA theories may unify different kinds of value and explain connections between value and reasons. Yet they face serious objections. Wrong-kind reasons can support an attitude without making its object valuable. Wrong-kind value cases suggest that value might exist without any possible valuer. Partiality challenges theories of comparative value. Circularity threatens accounts that explain all favorable responses by appealing to value.
key_ideas: Contemporary versions generally present FA theories as metaphysical accounts of evaluative properties and facts, not merely definitions of words.
A theory may target specific properties, such as admirability or delightfulness, general value, or both.
Theories differ over whether the relevant normative property is fittingness, reasons, rationality, obligation, justification, or another candidate.
Agent-neutral properties call for responses from anyone, while agent-relative properties may call for responses from particular people.
FA theories promise to unify diverse values, but their explanatory direction conflicts with views that take value to explain fitting responses.
Major challenges include wrong-kind reasons, wrong-kind value, partiality, and possible circularity.
summaries.why_it_matters: FA theories address a central question in value theory: what makes something good, admirable, lovable, or worth choosing? They offer a possible middle position between treating value as mysterious and treating it as nothing more than patterns of human reactions. Their success would provide a unified explanation of many evaluative properties and their connections with reasons. Their unresolved problems also show why philosophical theories must be tested against unusual cases, including coercion, absent valuers, personal attachments, and explanations that risk assuming what they aim to explain.

important_terms.definition: The normative relation in which a response stands to something when that thing merits or is worthy of the response.
A philosophical account that explains evaluative properties through normative facts about human responses.
The view that evaluative facts are fundamental and cannot be explained in other terms.
A view that explains evaluative properties entirely through non-normative facts about human responses.
A distinction between reasons that bear on an object's value and reasons that support an attitude without making its object valuable.
The proposal that value is a higher-order property grounded in other properties that provide reasons for favorable responses.

questions_to_think_about: Does explaining value through fitting responses clarify value, or does it merely rename the problem?
Can an FA theory distinguish a reason that makes something admirable from a threat that merely pressures someone to admire it?
Should a theory of value apply to worlds containing no beings capable of valuing?
Does a friend-relative reason make preferring a friend's rescue fitting, or does it only give a personal reason?
Can “positive response” be explained without already referring to value?

summaries.example: Imagine choosing between two rescue plans. The people involved are equal in every important way except that one is your close friend. You may reasonably prefer saving your friend, even if the two outcomes seem equally good overall. This is a challenge for a theory saying that one outcome is better whenever everyone ought to prefer it. Another challenge is a threat: if a villain says, “Praise this worthless object or I will hurt you,” the threat may give you a reason to praise it, but it may not make the object worthy of praise.
summaries.summary: Fitting-attitude theories, often called FA theories, try to explain value through normative facts about human responses. A response is fitting when its object merits or deserves it. Thus, one version might say that someone is admirable because admiration toward that person is fitting; another might say that something is valuable because there are reasons to value it. The theories can address specific values, such as being lovable or delightful, as well as value in general. They are different from primitivism, which treats value as fundamental, and from subjectivism, which explains value entirely through natural facts about what people respond to. Theories also face important choices. They must identify the relevant normative property, decide who should have the response, and determine whether their explanation is about properties, concepts, or meanings. A buck-passing account says that value itself does not add a separate reason to respond; instead, the features that make something valuable provide the reasons. Supporters think FA theories explain why value and appropriate responses seem closely connected, make value less mysterious, and bring many kinds of value into a common framework. Critics raise several problems. A threat can create a reason to praise something without making it praiseworthy. Value may appear to exist even where no possible person can respond. Personal relationships may make partiality fitting even when outcomes are equally good. Finally, an account of all positive responses may become circular if it explains “positive” by appealing to value.
key_ideas: FA theories say that evaluative facts depend on normative facts about responses that are appropriate or deserved.
A theory might explain admirability through fitting admiration, or general value through fitting valuing.
Philosophers disagree about whether to use fittingness, reasons, rationality, obligation, or another normative idea.
The theory must decide whether a response is required from everyone or only from particular agents.
FA theories may unify many forms of value, but rivals argue that value may instead explain fitting responses.
The main objections concern the wrong kind of reason, the wrong kind of value, favoritism, and circularity.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it examines how judgments about value connect with reasons, emotions, choices, and attention. It also tests whether a single theory can explain different ideas—such as good, admirable, delightful, or shameful—while respecting their differences. Studying the objections teaches an important philosophical skill: a theory must explain ordinary cases and also account for difficult cases that reveal hidden assumptions.

important_terms.definition: A response, such as admiration or enjoyment, that an object deserves or is worthy of receiving.
The quality of being good, valuable, admirable, lovable, delightful, or similar.
The relation between an object and a response when the object merits that response.
The view that value facts are basic rather than explained by other facts.
The view that value is fully explained by non-normative facts about human responses.
A theory that shifts the reason-giving work from value itself to other features that provide reasons for responses.

questions_to_think_about: If something is lovable because it deserves love, what makes the love deserved?
Are all reasons to have an attitude also reasons that make its object valuable?
Could something be valuable in a world where no one can value anything?
Does caring about a friend justify a preference, even when the options are equally good?
Can a theory explain what makes a response positive without using the idea of value?
